lessons.title: Nutritive Value of Korma
lessons.notes_html:
A Favourite and Popular Curry

Korma is one of the most favourite and popular curries, eaten with chapati or rice. It is full of nutrients because meat, ghee and spices are used in it.

Proteins in Meat

Meat is full of proteins, which are important for the growth and development of our body.

Fats Give Heat and Energy

The fats present in the meat provide heat and energy to the body.

Spices

Spices give taste to the curry, but excessive use of spices is harmful for health.

Key Points

  • Korma is a favourite and popular curry, eaten with chapati or rice.
  • Meat, ghee and spices are used in the korma.
  • Proteins are important for the growth and development of our body.
  • Fats present in the meat provide heat and energy to the body.
  • Spices give taste to the curry, but their excessive use is harmful for health.
  • Meat is full of nutrients — the statement "Meat has no nutrients" is false.

lessons.title: Recipe of Korma: Ingredients, Equipment and Method
lessons.notes_html:
Ingredients

Meat 1/2 kg; Ghee/Oil 125 gm (1/2 cup); Ginger (finely ground) 1 teaspoon; Garlic (finely ground) 1 teaspoon; Onions 2; Coriander powder 1 teaspoon; Red chilli powder 1-1/2 teaspoon; Black pepper powder 1/4 teaspoon; Cardamom (small) 2; Cardamom (large) 2; Cinnamon powder 1/4 teaspoon; Almonds 60 gms; Yogurt or tomatoes 125 gms; Salt to taste; Fresh coriander to taste.

Equipment

Stove, match-box, duster, degchi or cooking pan with lid, ladle, knife, cutting board, sieve, bowl, curry plate, curry bowl, serving spoon, quarter plate, tray with tray cover.

Method

(1) Peel and slice the onions. (2) Clean the meat and wash once or twice under running water. (3) Boil the almonds and peel off their skin. (4) Fry onions in ghee/oil until light brown. (5) Take out the onions and grind them. (6) Put onions, garlic, ginger and all the spices in ghee/oil and fry; add meat and fry till brown. (7) Add two cups of water and cook on low heat till the meat is tender. (8) Add yogurt or tomatoes and fry. (9) Add desired quantity of water and boil for 2-3 minutes. (10) Add almonds and coriander and cook for 2-3 minutes. (11) Korma is ready; pour it into the curry bowl. (12) Serve with chapaties or rice. Note: peeled almonds can be fried in ghee to make them crispy.

Key Points

  • A well-made korma is judged by: the meat is tender; spices and curry are well mixed; meat pieces are well browned.
  • The proportion of spices is accurate; the korma is tasty and well flavoured; it is served according to the instructions.
  • Onions are fried until light brown, taken out and ground before the meat is fried.
  • Yogurt or tomatoes (125 gms) are added after the meat becomes tender.

lessons.title: Nutrients in Pulao
lessons.notes_html:
A Favourite Dish

Pulao is a favourite dish among children and elders; its appearance and texture create interest on the dastarkhwan. Meat pulao and vegetable pulao are full of nutrients.

Rice — Carbohydrates

Rice is full of carbohydrates, which provide heat and energy to our body. Rice also contains some quantity of vitamin B, calcium and phosphorus, which are important for the normal functioning of our body.

Ghee or Oil — Fat

Ghee or oil provides fat, which gives energy and controls appetite.

Vegetables and Meat

Vegetables used in pulao provide vitamins and minerals to our body. Meat pulao provides proteins, iron and some vitamins, which control the wear and tear of cells and tissues and help in the growth and development of our body.

Key Points

  • Pulao is favourite among the children and the elders.
  • Rice is full of carbohydrates; old basmati rice is best for pulao.
  • Meat provides proteins and iron to our body.
  • Vegetables used in pulao provide vitamins and minerals.
  • Ghee has nutritive value — it provides fat and energy; the statement "Ghee has no nutritive value" is false.

lessons.title: Recipe of Pulao: Yakhni, Rice and Dum
lessons.notes_html:
Ingredients

Rice 1/2 kg or 2 cups; Meat 1/4 kg; Ghee/Oil 125 gms (1/2 cup); Whole spices 2 teaspoons; Aniseed (saunf) 2 teaspoons; Dry coriander 1 teaspoon; Ginger 15 gms; Onions 125 gms; Garlic 6-8 cloves; Cinnamon a 2.5 cm piece; Salt 1 teaspoon or to taste; Yogurt or tomatoes 100 gms; White cumin seeds 2 teaspoons.

Equipment

Stove, match-box, duster, spatula, degchi or cooking pan with lid, ladle, sieve, parat or tray, muslin cloth, knife, vegetable cutting board, plastic bowl, dish, dish spoon, plate, tablespoon, tray with tray cover.

Method

(1) Tie in a muslin cloth: one peeled and quartered onion, 6 crushed garlic cloves, coriander, cinnamon, aniseed and half the spices. (2) Wash the meat, put it in a pan with 8 cups of water and salt along with the muslin bag and cook on medium heat. (3) Pick, wash and soak the rice. (4) When the meat is tender, remove from heat. (5) Take out the tied spices and squeeze them thoroughly in the yakhni (stock). (6) Strain the yakhni and keep the meat in a bowl. (7) Slice the remaining onions and fry in ghee/oil. (8) Add meat, remaining spices, white cumin seeds, garlic and ginger and fry well; then add yogurt and fry. (9) Pour the yakhni in; add water if required (water must be double the quantity of the rice). (10) When the water boils, add rice, stir carefully with a spatula, cover and cook on high heat. (11) Watch till the water dries; then lower the heat and let the rice cook (dum); if a bit hard, steam on a tawa on low heat for 5-10 minutes. (12) Handle with a spatula carefully and remove from fire. (13) Serve in a dish with raita and salad.

Key Points

  • The whole spices for the yakhni are tied in a muslin cloth bag.
  • Water for pulao must be double the quantity of the rice.
  • A well-made pulao: rice tender and nicely coloured (brown), aroma increases appetite, meat tender, delicious and served well.

lessons.title: Nutrients in Shami Kababs
lessons.notes_html:
Proteins, Iron and Vitamin B

Proteins are present in meat and eggs, which are important for the metabolism of tissues and cells of the body. Iron and vitamin B are also present in the meat; iron is important for the growth of red blood cells.

Eggs and Dal Channa

Vitamin B and other minerals are present in the eggs and dal channa, which regulate the nervous and other systems of the body. Carbohydrates, proteins, vitamin B and minerals are present in the dal channa, which provide heat and energy.

Ghee and Spices

Fats and vitamin A and D are present in ghee, which provide heat and energy to our body. Spices increase aroma and stimulate appetite.

Vitamin C

Vitamin C is present in green coriander, green chillies and mint leaves.

Key Points

  • Dal channa is used in shami kababs (not dal masoor).
  • Fats, vitamin A and D are present in ghee or oil.
  • Iron is important for the growth of red blood cells.
  • Spices increase aroma and stimulate appetite.

lessons.title: Making Shami Kababs: Method and Serving
lessons.notes_html:
Ingredients

Minced meat 1/2 kg; Dal channa 125 gms; Ghee/Oil 1 cup (for frying); Spices powder 2 teaspoons; Red chilli powder 1/2 teaspoon; Green chillies as desired; Garlic (finely ground) 1/2 teaspoon; Onion (medium) 1; Ginger (finely ground) 1/2 teaspoon; Salt 3/4 teaspoon or to taste; Eggs 2; Cinnamon a 1.5 cm piece; Water 3 cups; White cumin seeds 1 teaspoon.

Equipment

Degchi or cooking pan with lid, stove, match-box, duster, knife, vegetable cutting board, plastic bowl, sieve, chopper, frying pan or tawa, spatula, plate, fork, dish, dish spoon, tray with tray cover.

Method

(1) Pick dal channa, wash and soak for half an hour. (2) Put dal channa, minced meat, garlic, ginger, onion, salt, red chilli powder, cinnamon, spices and water in a degchi; cook on medium heat. (3) When the meat and dal are tender and the water dries, take it off the fire. (4) Grind when it cools. (5) Beat the eggs in a bowl and mix them in the ground meat and dal; add green chillies, white cumin seeds and coriander and mix. (6) Make medium sized kababs, thick in the centre but thin at the sides. (7) Pour 2-3 tablespoons of ghee/oil in the frying pan; when hot, put kababs one by one and fry on low heat; when one side is brown, turn and fry the other side till brown. (8) Place the kababs on a newspaper to let the excess ghee be absorbed. (9) Spread tissue paper in a dish and put kababs on it. (10) Serve with tomato ketchup or mint chutney. Notes: minced meat should be washed under running water in a sieve to save its nutrients, colour and taste; kababs can also be made by dipping them in beaten eggs instead of mixing eggs in the meat; kababs are served on tissue paper to save their crispness.

Key Points

  • Kababs should be fried in a frying pan (or tawa) on low heat.
  • Kababs should be served by placing tissue paper in the plate; serve with tomato ketchup or mint chutney.
  • Well-made kababs: in their original shape (not broken), brown on all sides, correct proportion of spices, no extra fat, tasty, soft and crisp, properly served.

lessons.title: Halwa Sooji: Nutritive Value and Method
lessons.notes_html:
A Traditional Dish

Halwa Sooji is a favourite and popular dish for the young and the old in cities and villages; it is tasty, delicious and full of nutrients. It is part of our traditions and is distributed on special occasions like Shab-e-Mairaj and Shab-e-Barat, used at breakfast with puris on holidays and marriages, and served as a dessert after meals.

Nutritive Value

It is prepared from sugar, sooji, ghee and dry fruit: (1) Sooji contains carbohydrates, which provide heat and energy. (2) Sugar makes it delicious; it is full of calories and provides heat and energy. (3) Ghee is full of calories and fats, which provide heat and energy. (4) Vitamin A and D are present in the ghee, important for bones, skin and eye-sight. (5) Dry fruit makes it delicious and provides heat and energy; dry fruits are full of calories. Calories regulate our temperature and provide us energy to work; absence of these calories causes loss in weight.

Ingredients

Sooji 1/4 kg or one cup; Ghee or oil 80 gms or 1/2 cup; Sugar 1/4 kg or one cup; Almonds, pistachio, coconut, raisin 5 gms each; Silver leaves 2; Kewra 1 teaspoon; Water 3 cups; Cardamom 5.

Method

(1) Sift and clean the sooji. (2) Boil almonds in water, peel off and cut in thin pieces. (3) Clean raisins by removing their stems; cut pistachio and coconut. (4) Fry cardamom seeds in ghee on low heat. (5) Add sooji in it and fry. (6) When it is light brown and gives out a specific aroma, add half the dry fruit and mix. (7) Add sugar; when the sugar melts, add three cups of hot water and cook on high heat. When the water dries and the halwa gathers in the centre of the pan, take it off the fire. (8) Pour kewra in it and cover for 5 minutes. (9) Pour hot halwa in a dish, spread silver leaves on it and sprinkle the remaining dry fruit. (10) Serve hot in a tray with serving spoon, quarter plate and tablespoon.

Key Points

  • Halwa sooji is full of energy; sugar is used in it and ghee contains calories.
  • Vitamin A and D are important for health — for bones, skin and eye-sight.
  • Well-made halwa: light brown in colour, sooji well mixed with no lumps visible, correct proportion of ghee and sugar, delicious and full of aroma, decorated well and served properly.
  • Kewra (1 teaspoon) is poured in at the end and the halwa is covered for 5 minutes.

lessons.title: Fruit Jam: Nutritive Value and Rules of Jam Making
lessons.notes_html:
Preserving Fruits

Nature has gifted us with an abundance of fruits and vegetables. Fruits are eaten in their original form and are also preserved in the form of pickles, jams, chutneys and murrabbas; they add delicacy and colour to our dastarkhwan.

Nutritive Value of Jam

Fruit jam is very delicious and nutritious; at breakfast and in Ramazan we can take it with paratha or with bread. Fruit jam contains vitamins, carbohydrates and minerals, which provide heat and energy to our body and regulate the body systems.

Instructions about Jam Preparation

(1) Various fruits can be used for jam, e.g. pears, plums, mangoes, apricots, apples, guavas etc. (2) The fruit should be fresh, sour and free from blemishes. (3) Over-ripe or unripe fruits should be avoided. (4) Small sized fruit should be used whole, while large sized fruit should be cut into small pieces and boiled to make them tender. (5) Sugar and tartary should be used according to the condition of the fruit. (6) A well-prepared jam: its surface should be clear; it should not be thick or gummy but of desired consistency, i.e. neither thick nor hard; it should have its natural colour and aroma; the proportion of sugar and tartary should be appropriate. (7) Bottles should be sterilized.

Key Points

  • Fruit jam is very delicious and nutritious.
  • The fruit used for jam should be fresh and sour (and free from blemishes); over-ripe fruit is not best for jam.
  • Sugar and tartary should be used according to the fruit.
  • The bottles should be sterilized.
  • Preserve the jam in a dry and airy place.

lessons.title: Method of Fruit Jam and Sterilizing Bottles
lessons.notes_html:
Ingredients

Fruit (seasonal) 1 kg; Sugar 3/4 kg for sweet fruit and 1 kg for sour fruit; Lemon juice 28 gms or 2 tablespoons; Water 2 to 2-1/2 cups for less juicy fruit.

Equipment

Stainless steel degchi with lid, stove, matchbox, duster, pair of tongs, knife, vegetable cutting board, ladle and bottles with lids.

Sterilizing the Bottles

Wash bottles and lids thoroughly, place them in a degchi of water, boil for half an hour, take them out with tongs and place them upside down in a tray; when completely dry, fill the jam and seal.

Method

(1) Wash the fruit under running water. (2) Peel mangoes, plums, apples and pears; cut off their inner hard portion and soak them in a solution of 2-3% salt to maintain the colour of the fruit. (3) Cook juicy fruits with sugar in it for half an hour; less juicy fruits should be boiled in 2-1/2 cups of water to make them tender, then add sugar. (4) Cook on low heat till it boils; when it starts boiling, lower the heat and cook by constantly stirring. (5) When the mixture thickens, add lemon juice and cook for 8-10 minutes; in this way crystals of sugar will not be formed. (6) Take it off the fire and let it cool at 85 degrees C. Fill the jam in bottles, being careful that no bubbles are formed in the bottle. (7) Pour a melted paraffin wax layer on it and seal air-tight; it will keep the jam un-moistened. (8) Label and preserve the jam in a dry and airy place.

Key Points

  • No water is required for juicy fruits; less juicy fruits are boiled in water to make them tender.
  • While filling the jam in the bottle, be careful that no bubbles are formed in the bottle.
  • Well-made jam: fruit ripe, fresh and free from blemishes; fruit completely mixed; surface of the jam clean; jam soft and thick; bottles sterilized; bottles sealed properly.

lessons.title: Vegetable Pickle: Nutritive Value and Instructions
lessons.notes_html:
Why Preserve Vegetables as Pickles

Pickles are the favourite items served with meals; they not only increase appetite but also add delicacy to the meal. Vegetable pickle is mostly prepared at home; it is cheap and does not require much effort. Vegetables are available in abundance in season, are cheap and nutritious, so it is very beneficial to preserve them in the form of pickles.

Nutritive Value

Vegetables are good sources of vitamins and minerals. They do not provide much energy, but they add good taste to the food and provide roughage. They are called health-protecting food due to the presence of vitamins and minerals. Oil, vinegar and spices are used as preservatives; they retard the growth of micro-organisms and protect pickles from spoilage.

Selection of Vegetables

Vegetables should be fresh and free from blemishes; unripe vegetables are best for pickle; lemons used should be ripe; vegetables, oils and spices used should be of good quality.

Selection of Equipment

Plastic or stainless steel utensils should be used; use of metal utensils and spoons should be avoided; pickles should be preserved in a glass or polished earthenware jar or martaban; a wooden spoon should be used for taking out the pickle.

Precautions during Preservation

Sterilized martabans or jars should be used as containers; always cover the jar or martaban with a muslin cloth to avoid the growth of moulds and spoilage of pickle; use the desired quantity of oil in which the pickle is soaked well; always use a dry wooden spoon or ladle for taking out the pickle; take out only the desired quantity of pickle and never put the unused pickle back in the jar; always keep the pickle at a dry but airy place.

Vegetables Used for Pickles

Seasonal vegetables can be used for pickles, for example: cauliflower, carrots, turnips, radish, lemons, green chillies, bitter-gourds (karela), cabbage and onions.

Key Points

  • Pickles are the favourite items served with meal.
  • Lemons used for pickles should be ripe, while unripe vegetables are best for pickle.
  • Plastic or stainless steel utensils should be used for making the pickle.
  • A dry wooden spoon should be used for taking out the pickle.

Ingredients

(1) Wash all the vegetables and peel them; remove thin peels to avoid loss of nutrients. lessons.title: Drying Vegetables: Importance, Nutrients and Instructions
lessons.notes_html:
Importance of Dried Vegetables

Drying vegetables and fruits is one of the ancient methods of food preservation. Seasonal fruits and vegetables are available in abundance in their season; they are fresh, nutritious and cheap at that time, so it is beneficial and profitable to preserve them by drying. In this way we save money and also enjoy them in off-seasons. Dried vegetables keep their nutrients and can be stored for a long time in sterilized jars or cellophane bags; before cooking they are soaked in luke-warm water for thirty minutes.

Nutritive Value of Bitter-gourds

Bitter-gourds are popular vegetables of the summer season. They contain calcium, iron, phosphorus, proteins, vitamin B and vitamin C, and are very beneficial for diabetic patients. They can be cooked alone or with meat and minced meat, and can be preserved by drying.

Nutritive Value of Turnips

Turnips are available in abundance in the summer season; they can be eaten raw or in cooked form. Turnips contain phosphorus, proteins, calcium, vitamin C and iron. They can be cooked alone or with meat, and can be preserved by drying.

Instructions for Preserving by Drying

(1) Wash the vegetables and put them in clean utensils. (2) Peel them thinly and cut into small pieces. (3) Boil or steam the vegetables for some time and then spread in a tray or on a clean cloth. (4) Cover the vegetables with a clean muslin cloth to protect them from insects, flies and birds. (5) Different vegetables require different time for drying; thick vegetables like turnips and bitter-gourds take eight to ten days to dry completely. (6) To check the dryness of vegetables, press them in your hand; if they break easily, they have dried well. (7) Preserve dried vegetables in sterilized bottles, tins or cellophane bags, because sometimes small insects and bacteria develop in them during drying. (8) Keep them in a dry but cool place.

Key Points

  • Drying vegetables and fruits is one of the ancient methods of food preservation.
  • Sprinkle salt on bitter-gourds and dry them in the sun (after squeezing out the bitter water).
  • Bitter-gourds and turnips are soaked in a solution of potassium metabisulphite for twenty to thirty minutes.
  • Preserve bitter-gourds and turnips separately in the sterilized jars.
  • Dried vegetables do have flavour and taste — the statement "Dried vegetables have no flavour and taste" is false.

lessons.title: Method of Drying Bitter-gourds and Turnips
lessons.notes_html:
Ingredients

Bitter-gourds 1 kg; Turnips 1 kg; Potassium metabisulphite 6 gms for each vegetable; Salt 50 gms; Boiled water 2-1/2 litres for each vegetable.

Equipment

Saucepan, stove, match-box, duster, stainless steel parat or tray, knife, vegetable cutting board, mat, muslin cloth.

Method

(1) Wash bitter-gourds and turnips under running water. (2) Peel the turnips and cut into medium sized slices. (3) Scrape the bitter-gourds, cut into half lengthwise and into medium sized pieces, sprinkle salt on them and put them in the sun for ten minutes; squeeze the bitter-gourds, then wash under running water and squeeze. (4) Boil water in a saucepan; tie up the bitter-gourds in a muslin cloth and dip them in boiling water for 2-3 minutes, then take them out. (5) Again boil water; tie up the turnips in a muslin cloth and let them remain in boiling water for 2-3 minutes, then take them out. (6) Make a solution of 6 gms of potassium metabisulphite and water; soak the tied bundle of bitter-gourds in it for twenty to thirty minutes, then take it out and hang in the air. (7) In the same way, soak the turnips in a fresh solution for twenty to thirty minutes, take out and hang in the air. (8) Spread bitter-gourds and turnips in separate wire trays, cover with a muslin cloth and let them dry in the sun or in an airy place. (9) Turn the vegetables daily; they will dry completely in eight to ten days. (10) When completely dried, preserve separately in sterilized jars or martabans or in cellophane bags.

Key Points

  • Peel the turnips and cut into medium sized slices.
  • Sprinkle salt on bitter-gourds and put them in the sun for ten minutes, then squeeze them.
  • Soak bitter-gourds and turnips in a solution of potassium metabisulphite for twenty to thirty minutes.
  • Well-dried produce: dried well, neatly cut, soaked in the solution, fresh colour and natural aroma.

lessons.notes_html:
Chutneys in Eastern Meals

Vegetable and fruit chutneys are an important part of the eastern meals. In our country, tamarind, mint, pomegranate seeds, unripe mangoes, green chillies, onions, garlic, plums, apricots and tomato chutneys are mostly used. These chutneys are nutritious and good appetizers.

Nutritive Value

Chutneys prepared with fruits and vegetables are full of nutrients because minerals, vitamins and carbohydrates are present in them. Mango is considered to be the king of fruits; it has vitamins, minerals and carbohydrates which are necessary for the health, growth and development of the body.

Instructions about Chutneys

(1) Chutneys should be prepared in their season, because seasonal vegetables and fruits are fresh, cheap and nutritious. (2) Fruits and vegetables used should be plump and clean. (3) Spices used should be of good quality. (4) Sterilized bottles should be used. (5) Chutney should be cooked on low heat. (6) Spices used should be tied up in a muslin cloth to retain the colour of the fruit or vegetable; it should be well squeezed before taking it out. (7) Metal utensils should not be used; a wooden spoon should be used for stirring. (8) Chutneys should be preserved in a dry bottle and shaken once or twice so that no air bubbles are formed in it; it should be sealed with a wax covering.

Key Points

  • Fruit chutneys are nutritious and good appetizers.
  • Fruits and vegetables used for chutneys should be plump and clean.
  • Mango is the king of fruits.
  • Chutneys should be cooked on low fire.
  • Metal utensils should not be used for making the chutney.

Ingredients

Unripe mangoes 1 kg; Sugar 800 gms; Vinegar 100 gms; Salt 50 gms; Red chilli powder 15 gms; Whole spices 30 gms; Garlic 25 gms; Ginger (crushed) 20 gms; Onion 100 gms; Almonds 30 gms; Kalaunji 2 teaspoons.

Equipment

Stainless steel saucepan, stove, match-box, duster, wooden ladle, plastic sieve and bowl, knife, vegetable cutting board, muslin cloth, grater, sterilized bottle with cover.

Method

(1) Wash mangoes, peel and cut into small pieces or grate. (2) Pour half a cup of water in a saucepan, put mango pieces in it and let it boil twice or thrice so that the pieces become tender. (3) Tie up garlic, onion and spices in a muslin cloth. (4) Put the tied spices in the mango pieces and cook on low heat, constantly stirring with a wooden spoon. (5) When the mixture thickens, take it off the fire. (6) Take out the tied spices; when cool, squeeze it in the chutney. (7) Add vinegar, ginger and sugar and cook on low heat; when it thickens, add sliced almonds and take it off the fire. (8) When it cools, pour it in the sterilized bottle; shake it twice or thrice so that no bubbles are left in it; seal airtight and store in a cool dry place.

Key Points

  • Unripe mangoes (1 kg) are used, with sugar 800 gms and vinegar 100 gms.
  • Garlic, onion and spices are tied in a muslin cloth and cooked with the mango pieces on low heat.

lessons.title: Health and the Factors of Good Health
lessons.notes_html:
What is Health

Good health is the essence of life; it helps in enjoying the ultimate values related to the human body. Health means mental and physical well-being. A person is considered healthy when all parts of the body are working normally and there is no feeling of unnecessary fatigue. The individual feels hail and hearty, full of enthusiasm and life and mental alertness; he participates in social welfare programmes with interest, is free from worries and is capable of maintaining good relations with everyone.

Factors of Good Health

(1) Balanced diet — it maintains the grace, beauty and health of various parts of the body; we should use milk and milk products, cereals, grains, fats, fruits and vegetables, meat, fish and eggs in our daily diet. (2) Proper exercise — inhalation of fresh and clean air early in the morning, morning walk, walk after the evening meal, P.T. and drill in schools and races are necessary for freshness of mind, circulation of blood and expansion of lungs. (3) Body cleanliness — cleanliness of the hands, nails, teeth, hair, eyes, ears and nose along with the rest of the body. (4) Treating of the foul smell — covered parts of the body (mouth, armpits, feet) should be cleaned properly; bath is necessary for removing foul smell; deodorant or talcum powder should be used after bath. (5) Clean and proper dress — dress protects and covers our body and enhances our personality; it should be according to the personality, daily activities, age, occasion and climate. (6) Proper sleep and rest — extremely necessary to keep oneself fit after the long strenuous work of a day. (7) Interesting leisure time hobbies — hobbies should be interesting and such activities should be adopted which do not have any harmful effect on health.

Key Points

  • Good health is the essence of life, and very important to get the best out of one's personality.
  • Dress enhances our personality, and we should wear neat and proper dress.
  • Adequate sleep is necessary for health.
  • Body cleanliness includes cleanliness of the hands, nails, teeth, hair, eyes, ears and nose along with the rest of the body.

lessons.notes_html:
Hands and Nails

Cleanliness and beauty of the hands adds to the charm of the personality; the skin of the hands should be properly cared for. Nails should be cleaned daily; dirty nails are harmful for health and give a dirty look; nails should be trimmed and filed properly once a week so that no dirt or grease gathers in them.

Teeth

Teeth are an important part of our face, visible while talking or laughing; if dirty they give a bad impression and are harmful for the gums and stomach. Eat a balanced diet including milk (calcium is necessary for healthy growth and structure of teeth); avoid sweets because they lead to cavities and loss of lustre; brush teeth thoroughly and regularly before and after breakfast and after every meal.

Eyes

Eyes are an important part of the body and are considered the index of one's personality. A balanced diet is necessary; adequate sleep according to age is necessary (inadequate sleep causes swelling of the eyelids, black circles under the eyes and loss of glow); sufficient light should be used while reading or working — dim light strains the eyes; do not read in a moving car or bus; sit straight and keep the book at a distance of one foot to one and a half feet; periodical checkup by a qualified doctor and eye-specialist is necessary.

Hair

Wash hair once or twice a week; soap is harmful for hair — wash with a mild shampoo and rinse under running water several times; a balanced diet (fruits, vegetables, milk, meat) makes hair soft and firm; massage with oil is necessary for dry hair; wash oily hair several times; always comb or brush properly, as combing is necessary for circulation of blood and healthy growth of hair.

Ears

Ears should be cleaned with a soft cloth or towel while taking a bath.

Key Points

  • Nails should be cleaned daily and trimmed and filed properly once a week.
  • A balanced diet is necessary for eyes, and eyes are the index of one's personality.
  • Teeth are an important part of our face.
  • A well-groomed student: properly washed hands and face, well-combed and brushed hair, proper dress, neat and free from wrinkles, takes interest in the upkeep of her personality.

lessons.title: Darning and Patchwork
lessons.notes_html:
Darn and Patch

Garments used daily sometimes require repair because of a tear or a hole caused by insects or due to the weakening of the fabric. Darning is the method of mending a small hole by weaving new threads across it with a needle, following the warp and weft of the fabric; darning is the best method for mending small holes. Patchwork is done by covering the hole with a similar fabric; a patch can be made in round, oval, square or triangular shape, and it is more suitable for mending a large hole. The patch should be applied according to the direction of the cloth; in designed or striped fabric, the patch should follow the same direction of the design or stripes.

Steps of Darning

(1) The thread used should be according to the kind and colour of the fabric. (2) A single strand of thread should be used; a double strand can be used according to the thickness of the fabric. (3) A knot should not be used. (4) A long-headed fine needle should be used for taking small stitches. (5) Darning can be done in round, square or oval shapes. (6) Running stitches should be taken at a distance of 0.5 cm from the edge of the hole. (7) Lengthwise filling of threads should be done first, then cross-wise filling. (8) Filling should be according to the fabric. (9) Filling should neither be loose nor tight. Precautions: follow the lengthwise and cross-wise grains of the fabric; leave a little thread extra after filling; the direction of the needle should be left to right and right to left.

Method of Darning a Tear

Make a square tear of 2 x 2 cms in the centre of a 15 x 15 cms cotton piece; mark with tailor's chalk 0.5 cm all around the hole; frame the fabric with the hole in the centre; take small running stitches from left to right, lengthwise; then make a series of stitches crossing the lengthwise stitches, taking one thread under and one thread over, as in plain weave; filling should be close according to the weave; unscrew the frame and iron the darn.

Method of Patchwork

(1) Trim the hole to be patched in the desired shape. (2) Cut the cloth to be patched about 2.5 cms larger than the hole and clip it diagonally at about 1 cm from the corners. (3) Cut the cloth to be used for patching with 1/2 cm seam allowance; place it on a flat surface with the wrong side facing the fabric and pin it. (4) Place the cloth to be patched on it so that it matches with the design and the grainline, and pin it. (5) Baste it about 1.5 cms from the edge of the hole; remove the pins. (6) Turn the cloth and hem it with close stitches. (7) Turn the cloth on the wrong side and hem the edges on all sides; the stitches should not be visible on the right side.

Key Points

  • Small holes are mended by darning; large holes are mended by using a patch.
  • Matching thread (according to the kind and colour of the fabric) should be used for darning.
  • Good darning: proper thread, correct method, neat work, parallel to the warp and weft yarns, no flare in the finished darning.
  • Good patchwork: patch neatly cut, warp and weft yarns straight, edges basted, hemmed stitches not visible on the right side.

lessons.title: Buttonholes and Buttons
lessons.notes_html:
Types of Buttonholes

Buttonholes are made on double tape and in horizontal and vertical positions. Blanket or buttonhole stitch is used for making buttonholes, and a lot of practice is required to achieve neatness. There are two types: (a) Vertical buttonholes — a bar of thread is made at both the ends. (b) Horizontal buttonholes — a bar of thread is made at one end and a fan is made at the other end.

Method of Making a Buttonhole

On a piece of cotton cloth 10 x 15 cms: (1) Fold the cloth lengthwise and mark a centre line. (2) Machine stitch or hand stitch on this line. (3) Cut along the basting and overcast. (4) Make buttonhole stitch from right to left. (5) Finish one end of the buttonhole by forming a bar tack. (6) Continue with buttonhole stitch along the opposite side and finish with a bar-tack. (7) Cut the thread; the buttonhole is complete.

Types of Buttons

Buttons are used for fastening garments, e.g. on necklines and cuffs; they are sewed on the double thickness of cloth. The three basic types are: (1) Snaps, (2) Shirt buttons, (3) Link buttons. Besides these, there are decorative buttons made of plastic, steel or metal, plain, coloured, embossed or decorative. Snaps have two parts: one part has a rounded extension which fits into the other part which has a hollow space; the part with the rounded extension is sewed on the side overlapping the tape (upper tape) and the other part on the lower side. Shirt buttons have two or four holes; they are sewed on the lower tape while buttonholes are made on the upper tape; they are sewed with a double strand of thread, and the thread is wound under the button to form a stem or shank and fastened securely. Link buttons are used as links for joining the upper and lower parts of the cuffs; the thread is run through the two buttons and worked over with blanket stitch to make a thread bar.

Key Points

  • A bar (of thread / bar tack) is made at the ends of the buttonholes.
  • Snaps consist of two parts; the rounded extension of the snap is kept on the upper tape.
  • Buttonholes are made on a double layer of cloth, not a single layer.
  • The button should be fastened securely before cutting the thread.
  • Decorative buttons are not simple — they may be plain, coloured, embossed or decorative.

lessons.title: Gathers, Pleats and the Flat Fell Seam
lessons.notes_html:
Importance of Gathers

Gathers are used in a dress to create soft, even folds. The basic purpose of gathers is to produce ease and to create beauty in a dress. Gathers are mostly used on children's dresses, on cuffs, yokes and shirts etc. Gathering can be done by stitching with a needle (by hand) or with a machine: a double strand of thread is used for gathering by hand, whereas a long machine stitch is used for gathering by machine.

Gathering by Machine

Increase the size of the stitch by adjusting the stitch regulator; make a row of machine stitch at the seamline to be gathered, leaving about 5 cms of thread at each end; make another row of stitches 1 cm away from the first stitching line; make a knot at one end by joining the threads from both rows; draw or pull the threads with the right hand and keep pushing the stitches together slowly and carefully from both rows with the left hand; even the gathers by pressing softly along the seamline and stitch.

Ways of Making Pleats

Pleats are used to make a dress look beautiful; an important function of pleats is to create fullness, and pleats also add beauty and fitness to the dress. Pleats are used at necklines, yokes, shoulders and the front or back side, and are mostly used on children's frocks. Pleats are made in three ways: (1) Side pleats — all folds turned to one side; the width of all folds should be the same, or a little less on one side and more on the other. (2) Box pleats — made on the right side of the fabric by pressing the fold from the centre and stitching it on the right and left side of the fold from the centre. (3) Inverted pleats — made on the wrong side of the fabric by turning two folds away from each other but meeting at the centre.

Flat Fell Seam

The flat fell seam is a seam mostly used on thick cloth. It has no wrong or right side, therefore it is mostly used for joining bedsheets. It is a durable seam and is most useful for men's or children's pants, trousers, knickers and shirts etc. Method: (1) Match the wrong sides of the material together and pin. (2) Mark 2 cms seam allowance and stitch. (3) Trim one edge of the cloth at the centre. (4) Turn the other edge over the trimmed edge; baste, press and stitch.

Key Points

  • The basic purpose of gathers is to produce ease and beauty in the dress.
  • Gathering can be done by stitching with a needle or with a machine.
  • Pleats add beauty and fitness to the dress, and create fullness.
  • Good gathering: proper material, straight stitching lines, even and smooth division of gathers, beautiful after finishing.
  • Good flat fell seam: correct method, proper material, correct width of seam, neat stitches, smooth and flat seam.

lessons.title: Importance of Measurements and Points to Keep in Mind
lessons.notes_html:
Importance of Taking Measurements

Proper stitching of a dress depends, to a great extent, upon accurate cutting. For accurate cutting, correct measurements of the body are required. The elegant fitting of the dress depends upon the proper measurements, which add to the beauty of a dress.

Points to Keep in Mind while Giving Measurements

It is not possible to take accurate measurements by oneself, therefore the following points should be kept in mind while giving the measurements: (1) Measurements should be given by wearing a light dress; loose and heavy weight dress should be avoided. (2) Stand straight but at ease; take off dopatta and tie up your hair. (3) Keep a notebook and a pencil with you so as to note down the measurements. (4) All measurements should be a bit loose and not tight; ease allowance should be added in the draft. Note: check these measurements from time to time.

Key Points

  • The fitting of a well-stitched dress depends upon the proper measurements.
  • Tie up your hair while taking measurements.
  • Take all measurements a bit loose and not tight.
  • The statement "It is possible to take accurate measurements by oneself" is false.
  • The statement "Fitting is not affected by inaccurate measurements" is false.
  • Good measurement taking: body straight and at ease, light weight dress worn, position of the tape correct, method of noting the measurements correct.

lessons.title: Method of Taking Body Measurements
lessons.notes_html:
Across Back

Measure from one shoulder to the other shoulder by keeping the tape over the back of the shoulders; note it in the notebook; keep the tape on the right points, otherwise shoulder fitting will be affected.

Centre-back Length

Measure from the top of the prominent bone at the base of the neck to the natural waistline; this measurement is required for making darts in a shirt, and incorrect measurements will have adverse effects on proper fitting.

Bust

Measure around the body at the fullest part of the bust; join the ends of the tape in the centre and note the measurement; keep the tape in correct position across the back and in front.

Waist

Measure around the body at the waist by placing two finger tips inside the tape.

Hips

Measure around the fullest and widest part of the hips, approximately 20 cms below the natural waistline.

Full Length

The length of the shirt changes according to the fashion; keep the tape at the shoulder top and measure up to the desired length.

Sleeves

Length and width of the arm are required for sleeves. For the length of the sleeve, place the tape at the shoulder and measure up to the wrist with the arm a little bent at the elbow (if sleeves are to be made 3/4, keep the arm straight). For the width of the sleeve, place the tape all around the wrist and measure.

Key Points

  • Bring the tape straight (level) around the body.
  • Bust measurement is taken over the fullest part of the bust.
  • Hips measurement is taken approximately 20 cms below the natural waist line.
  • The statement "All measurements should be taken from right side" is false.

lessons.title: The Kurta: Measurements and Parts of the Draft
lessons.notes_html:
About the Kurta

Kurta is a loose dress; it is quite suitable for summer wear. In a kurta all seams are straight, and it is mostly made of sheer fabrics, e.g. muslin, lawn, voile etc. Mostly the draft of a kurta is not made, but for learning it is important to make the draft of the kurta on brown paper.

Measurements Required for the Draft

(1) Across-back, (2) Bust, (3) Full length, (4) Sleeves. The standard measurements of a thirteen years old girl given in the chapter are: Across-back 30 cms (12 inches); Bust 76 cms (30 inches); Full length 90 cms (36 inches); Sleeve length 46 cms (18 inches). One should use one's own measurements to make the draft of a kurta for oneself.

Parts of the Draft

The draft of the kurta is made in four parts: (1) Centre panel, (2) Kali, (3) Gusset, (4) Sleeve. The drafts of the front and back centre panel are the same but are made separately due to the shape of the front and back necklines; the drafts of kali, gusset and sleeve are made separately and in one piece.

Details of the Draft

Centre panel: draw a vertical line A to C, AC = 90 cms (full length); draw a horizontal line A to B, AB = 15 cms (1/2 across-back); join ABCD and mark the foldline on line AC. Front neckline: on line AC measure 7.6 cms from A and mark K (AK = 1/10 bust); on line AB measure 7.6 cms from A and mark L; join K with L in a curve. Back neckline: on line AC measure 2.5 cms from A and mark M; on line AB measure 7.6 cms from A and mark N; join M with N in a curve. Sleeve: draw a vertical line AB = 16 cms (width of the sleeve); draw horizontal lines A to C and B to D, AC and BD = 46 cms (length of the sleeve); join C with D and mark the foldline at line AC. Kali: draw a vertical line A to B, AB = 74 cms (full length minus width of the sleeve); for the upper part draw a horizontal line A to C, AC = 6.4 cms (1/12 bust); for the lower part draw a horizontal line B to D, BD = 13 cms; join B with D. Gusset: make a square ABCD = 6.4 cms; fold it during stitching. Seam allowance is marked on all parts of the draft.

Key Points

  • Kurta is a loose dress and all seams of kurta are straight.
  • Mostly the draft of a kurta is not made, but it is made on brown paper for learning.
  • The draft of the front and back centre panel of kurta is the same.
  • Cotton fabric is the best material for learning the stitching of a kurta.
  • Good drafting: lines of the paper parallel to the lines of the draft, sharp pencil used, all markings made, each part labelled, front and back necklines clearly made.

lessons.title: Cutting and Stitching the Kurta
lessons.notes_html:
Steps of Cutting

(1) For learning, it is necessary to use an inexpensive material; cotton fabric is best for this purpose. Shrink the material before cutting: soak the material in water for a few hours, squeeze it, let it dry, then press it. (2) Fold the cloth lengthwise; pin the drafts of the front and back panel separately on it, mark seam allowances and cut from the sides. (3) Fold the cloth twice, pin the draft of the sleeve on it, mark seam allowances and cut. (4) Fold the cloth twice, pin the draft of the gusset on it, mark seam allowances and cut. (5) Fold the cloth, pin the draft of the kali on it, mark seam allowances and cut. (6) Fold the cloth for cutting the front neckline facing at a distance of 2.5 cms; cut the back neckline by following the same method. (7) For making a buttontape, mark 6 cms from the centre towards the right side and mark a 20 cms long cut; slash a little on both sides of its end. (8) Cut two strips of 4 x 23 cms and 7.5 cms respectively for the buttontape.

Stitching of the Kurta

(1) Join the front and back centre panel at the shoulder seamline and stitch. (2) Making the neckline: join the front and back neckline facing and stitch; place them on the right side of the front and back neckline and stitch; slash small tucks and turn it towards the wrong side, pin, baste and hem. (3) Pin the 4 x 23 cms wide strip on the extended side of the opening and stitch; fold the strip to the inside by keeping 1 cm on the right side and hem. (4) Pin the 7.5 x 23 cms strip on the right side of the opening and stitch; turn by keeping 2.5 cms on the right side and hem. (5) Overlap the narrow side and hem to make the centre of the point; make buttonholes on the upper buttontape and sew buttons on the lower buttontape. (6) Joining kali, gusset and sleeve: stitch the straight sides of the kali at the top with one side of the gusset; turn the gusset from the centre and stitch it with the second kali; stitch the sleeve with gusset and kali from one side and then from the other side; join the other sleeve in the same way. (7) Now join them with the centre panel and stitch. (8) Hem; the kurta is complete.

Key Points

  • Cotton fabric is the best material for learning the stitching of a kurta, and the cloth is shrunk before cutting.
  • Good cutting: cloth shrunk before cutting, cloth straight, cutting done keeping the cloth lengthwise, all parts cut smooth and even according to the measurements, selvedge present on the sleeve.
  • Good stitching: gusset stitched with the kalis; kalis stitched with the sleeves; kalis and sleeves neatly stitched with the centre panel; neckline round; buttonhole tape neatly finished; kurta hemmed neatly.
  • Buttonholes are made on the upper buttontape and buttons sewed on the lower buttontape.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 — Shalwar: Drafting, Cutting and Stitching (Health and Stitching, Ch 6)

lessons.title: The Shalwar Draft: Paenchahas and Kundas
lessons.notes_html:
About the Shalwar

Shalwar is stitched in two ways: plain shalwar and shalwar with a belt. In a plain shalwar the length of paenchahas and kundas is the same. In a shalwar with a belt, the length of the belt is deducted from the total length, while the total length of the kundas and paenchahas is kept the same. The draft of a shalwar is required just for learning; after getting practice, it is not needed.

Measurements Required

(1) Total length, (2) Crotch, (3) Width of the paenchah. The presumed measurements used in the chapter are: Total length = 100 + 5 cms (naifa) = 105 cms; Crotch = 45 cms (1/2 length minus 5 cms); Width of the paenchah = 30 cms (1/4 length + 5 cms).

Parts of the Draft

The draft of a plain shalwar is made in two parts: (1) Paenchahas, and (2) Kundas. Length of the paenchah = total length of the shalwar + 5 cms for naifa. Width of the paenchah = required width of the paenchah minus 2.5 cms. Length of the kunda = length of the paenchah + crotch + 5 cms. Width of the kunda = 5 to 7 cms more than the width of the paenchah.

The Draft in Detail

Paenchah draft: draw a vertical line A to C, AC = total length of the shalwar = 105 cms; draw horizontal lines A to B and C to D, BD = width of the paenchah = 30 cms; join ABCD; measure 5 cms downwards from AB for naifa; add 1.2 cms seam allowance all around ABCD. Kundas draft: draw a horizontal line A to B, AB = 45 cms; draw a vertical line A to C, AC = paenchah + crotch + 5 cms = 105 + 45 + 5 = 155 cms; complete the rectangle ABCD; from A measure 50 cms downwards and mark G (AG = crotch + naifa); from D measure 50 cms upwards and mark H; measure 2.5 cms inwards from G and H and mark K, L; join K, L in a slanting line; measure 5 cms downwards from AB and 5 cms upwards from CD for naifa; mark 2.5 cms seam allowance all around ABCD.

Width of Kundas — the Formula

The formula used for calculating the upper width of the kunda is: width of the kunda = 1/2 of the total length of the shalwar. For example, if the total length of the shalwar is 100 cms, the width of the kunda should be 100 x 1/2 = 50 cms. The lower width of the kunda should be 5 to 7 cms more than the width of the paenchah. This formula can be used for making a draft for any age-group.

Key Points

  • Shalwar is made in two ways: plain shalwar and shalwar with a belt.
  • In a plain shalwar the length of the paenchahas and kundas is according to the total length.
  • The draft of a plain shalwar is made in two parts.
  • The statement "Length of the kunda is added in the total length of the shalwar" is false.
  • Good drafting: paenchah and kunda measurements calculated according to the formula; crotch size according to the formula; all lines clear; lines marked correctly; all parts labelled properly.

lessons.title: Cutting and Stitching the Plain Shalwar
lessons.notes_html:
Cutting

Two paenchahas and four kundas are required for making a shalwar. Fold the cloth according to its width for paenchahas, pin the draft of the paenchah on it and cut two paenchahas. Fold the cloth again, pin the draft of the kunda on it and cut four kundas.

Stitching

Stitching of the plain shalwar is very easy: (1) Joining the kundas — join the lengthwise sides of one paenchah with the sides of the kundas; follow the same method for the other paenchah; stitch the crotch from the centre. (2) Stitching of the naifa — turn the naifa on the seamline, fold the cloth 0.5 cms and stitch. (3) Making the paenchahas — the facing for the paenchahas will be according to the length and width of the paenchahas and the same material and colour will be used; the buckram facing will be according to this size; on the right side of the shalwar place the facing and buckram and stitch; turn it towards the wrong side and make rows of stitches according to the fashion or as desired. (4) Stitching the sides of the shalwar — after making the paenchahas, stitch from the sides; the shalwar is complete.

Key Points

  • Stitching of a plain shalwar is easy — the statement "Stitching of a plain shalwar is very difficult" is false.
  • The sides of the shalwar are stitched after making the paenchahas, not before — the statement "Sides should be stitched before making paenchahas" is false.
  • Good stitching: lengthwise side of the paenchah joined with the kundas; crotch stitched properly from the centre; naifa turned and stitched neatly; finished paenchahas neat; side stitching correct.
  • Before cutting: cloth is shrunk, ironed after shrinking, kept at lengthwise grain; drafts pinned properly; paenchahas and kundas neatly cut.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 — Removing Spots and Stains from the Fabrics (Living in the Family, Ch 1)

lessons.title: Types of Stains and Methods of Removing Them
lessons.notes_html:
Types of Stains

Sometimes a fabric gets stains if handled carelessly; the stain is absorbed in the fabric and spoils it. Some stains are easily removed by washing with soap and water, while some require special treatment. Stains are classified according to their nature: (1) Stains of animal source — stains of meat, blood, egg and milk have protein properties; these should not be washed with hot water. (2) Stains of plant and vegetable source — stains of tea, coffee, fruit and vegetable are acidic in nature, therefore alkaline chemicals should be used for removing them. (3) Stains of oil and grease — stains of ghee, cream, butter, curry, oil and varnish are removed by using solvents which can dissolve the fats. (4) Stains of mineral source — stains of rust, black ink and medicines are composed of metals and pigments; these are first treated with an acidic solution to dissolve the metal, then soaked in an alkaline solution to remove the acidic left-over stain. (5) Stains of colours — during laundering, the colour of certain clothes stains the other clothes; these might be acidic or alkaline, so they should be removed carefully. (6) Stains of grass — grass stains are of vegetable source but require special care and treatment due to the presence of chlorophyll.

Methods of Removing Stains

(1) Soaking or dipping method — the easiest method; the whole cloth or the stained portion is soaked or dipped in the stain removing agent and then washed with soap and water. (2) Steaming method — used for removing stains of coloured silken and woollen fabrics; the clothes are first steamed, then placed over a blotting paper and pressed with a hot iron; the stain is absorbed by the blotting paper. (3) Dropping method — the stain removing agent is dropped on the stain with a dropper, placing a blotting paper or absorbent cloth under the stain. (4) Sponging method — commonly used in our homes; a blotting paper or absorbent cloth is kept under the stained fabric and the stain is removed by rubbing with a soft pad dipped in the solvent, with small strokes from the outer side of the stain to the inner side in circles, then pressed with a steam iron; change the pad and blotting paper for better results.

Principles of Removing Stains

(1) If some liquid drops on the cloth, it should be immediately washed or absorbed with a cloth or a blotting paper. (2) The nature of the stain should be noted so as to use the right solvent at the right time. (3) The stain should not be pressed with the fingers, because it will be absorbed in the fibre. (4) The solvent should be first tested on a small piece or hidden part of the garment before application.

Key Points

  • A fabric gets stained if handled carelessly.
  • Hot water should not be used for removing blood stains (animal-source/protein stains).
  • The stains of vegetable source have acidic characteristics.
  • Blotting paper should be used for absorbing the stain — the statement that it should not be used is false.
  • Good stain removal: all stains removed properly, according to the instructions, the stained portion not damaged, surface of the cloth smooth, chemicals used according to the types of the stain.

lessons.title: Stain-removing Agents and Removing Particular Stains
lessons.notes_html:
Agents and Chemicals

(1) Water — a neutral agent which absorbs and removes all types of stains except the stains of fat; used on all types of fabrics; stains on nylon and dacron fabrics are easily removed by washing with lukewarm water and soap. (2) Carbon tetra chloride — a harmless chemical used for removing all types of grease stains. (3) Bleaches — mild solutions of sodium hydrosulphite, hydrogen peroxide and oxalic acid are used for removing stains of coloured fabrics. (4) Amyl-acetate — very effective for removing stains of paint and nail-polish, but it dissolves the acetate fibres. (5) Ammonia — it has a soap-like action; it can be used for removing all types of stains except stains of grease; it should be washed immediately after use. (6) Glycerine — used for removing fruit and vegetable stains; it should be immediately washed with soap and water after use.

Removing Particular Stains

Grass stain: take kerosene oil or alcohol or methylated spirit in a bowl; soak the stained portion in it for five minutes; wash with soap and water and dry in the sun. Tea stain: pour boiling water on the fresh stain, wash with soap and water and dry in the sun; for a moist old stain, rub borax powder on it, wash with soap and water and dry in the sun. Ink stain: soak the stain in one cup of milk for thirty minutes; wash with soap and water and dry in the sun; the ink stain can also be removed by rubbing lemon and salt on it. Curry stains: soak the stained portion in a solution of soap and hot water for five minutes, rub and wash; if not removed completely, soak in a bleach for some time, wash thoroughly and dry in the sun. Blood stains: wash the fresh stain under running water; for old stains, make a solution of three tablespoons of salt in one cup of water, soak the stained portion for fifteen minutes, rub and wash with soap and water, dry in the sun; a mild solution of ammonia can also be used.

Key Points

  • Water is a neutral solvent; carbon tetra chloride does not remove stains of grass — it removes grease stains.
  • Glycerine is used for removing fruit and vegetable stains.
  • Mild bleach (mild solution of sodium hydrosulphite, hydrogen peroxide and oxalic acid) is used for removing stains from coloured woollen and silken clothes; the steaming method is also used for such fabrics.
  • Amyl-acetate removes paint and nail-polish stains but dissolves acetate fibres.

lessons.title: Washing and Ironing Shirt, Shalwar and Dopatta
lessons.notes_html:
Why Wear Neat and Clean Dress

Dress not only covers the body and protects it from severe hot and cold weather, it also reflects our taste and refinement. A neat and clean dress enhances our personality. School-going girls should wear a neat and clean uniform daily; it should be changed immediately after reaching home and should be washed daily, because a dirty dress develops bad odour.

Equipment for Washing

Before washing, check that no part of the garment is worn out, the zip or buttons of the shirt are closed and the shalwar is without tape or elastic (mended before washing). Equipment: (1) A small tub. (2) Soap and indigo for bluing. (3) Starch — starch is used for cotton clothes only; prepare the starch by mixing three tablespoons of maida with one cup of cold water, boil by stirring constantly until it thickens, remove from the stove and use when it cools.

Method of Washing

(1) Take water in a tub; put the dopatta in it; apply soap and rub the stained parts especially; rinse in clean water and keep it aside. (2) If the soapy water is not dirty, wash the shirt in the same water, otherwise change it; rub the necklines and cuffs especially; rinse in clean water and keep aside. (3) Wash the shalwar in the same way with special rubbing of its paenchahas; rinse in clean water and keep aside. (4) White clothes are treated with bluing for lustre and whiteness: mix bluing (indigo) in water, add some starch, mix well and soak the dopatta in it for three to four minutes; then wring it out and shake. (5) Add some more starch and indigo, soak the shirt in it for five minutes; wring out and shake. (6) Add some more starch and indigo and soak the shalwar in it for five minutes; wring out and shake. (7) Clean the drying string and spread the shalwar, dopatta and shirt on it properly by removing the wrinkles with hands. (8) Replace all the equipment at its proper place and wash the working area.

Ironing

Clothes are ironed to attain the maximum glow and finish. Be careful while using any type of iron, because clothes can be scorched due to careless handling; never use the iron with wet hands, and the wire should not be worn out because it might cause a direct electric shock. Method: (1) Clothes with starch require a little moisture for ironing, so remove the clothes when they are a little damp; otherwise sprinkle some water to dampen them and fold them for some time. (2) If there is no ironing board, spread some clean thick cloth or blanket on the table. (3) Set the dial of the iron on the number for cotton clothes. (4) Iron the dopatta first lengthwise and then widthwise; fold it or hang it on a hanger. (5) Iron the sleeves of the shirt first, then the front and back side of the shirt; fold or hang on a hanger. (6) The shalwar needs careful ironing as it has more starch: iron one side, then the other side; iron the paenchah and naifa from both sides; keep both the paenchahas together and iron; fold or hang on hangers.

Key Points

  • A neat and clean dress reflects our taste and refinement and enhances our personality.
  • The neckline and cuffs of the shirt should be rubbed specially during washing.
  • The use of bluing whitens the white clothes.
  • Good washing and ironing: clothes mended before washing; washed clothes clean; indigo and starch used properly; clothes ironed after dampening; clothes ironed properly.

Method of Washing the Sweater

(1) Shake off the sweater. (2) Sketch out its shape on a brown paper. (3) Make suds by mixing two to three tablespoons of washing powder and luke-warm water; put the sweater in it and rub gently. (4) Take out the sweater by holding it between your hands just like a bowl and rinse it under running water. (5) Place it on the sketched outline and let it dry on a flat surface. (6) Let it dry in an open and shady place; do not dry in direct sunshine. (7) Remove from the brown paper, dry and fold. (8) Iron it, if required, with a warm iron with muslin cloth on it. (9) Brush it, if required.

Key Points

  • The outline of the sweater is drawn on the brown paper before washing.
  • Luke-warm water is used for washing the sweater.
  • The sweater is rinsed according to the instructions and the water is squeezed properly.
  • The sweater is dried on a flat surface, in an open and shady place — not in direct sunshine.
  • Clothes do not lose lustre by ironing (the book's true/false marks this statement true — ironing gives glow and finish).

lessons.title: Cleanliness of the Kitchen and the Gas Stove
lessons.notes_html:
Why Clean the Kitchen

The kitchen is an important place in the house. The health of the family depends upon the overall cleanliness as well as the cleanliness of the food cooked there. The kitchen should be cleaned twice or thrice a day. A neat and clean kitchen not only looks attractive but also reflects the taste of the housewife.

Points while Cleaning the Kitchen

(1) The dustbin should be cleaned after the work is over; it should be washed and kept upside down to prevent the bad odour. (2) A separate cloth should be kept aside for cleaning the working area or working table; it should be first wiped with a dry cloth and then with a wet cloth to remove any grains of food spilled there. (3) All the utensils used should be washed with soap or vim, dried and then kept at their proper places. (4) The equipment used for cooking should be arranged at their proper places. (5) The stove gets the spots and stains of ghee, milk, atta etc.; if these spots are not cleaned after finishing the work, a layer of dirt is formed on it, therefore it should be cleaned with a wet cloth after use. (6) The floor of the kitchen should be washed with hot water; the dustbin should be washed and dried in the sun; sink and water taps should be washed; if there are open drains in the kitchen, wash them thoroughly and pour phenyl in them; after cleaning, it should be left open for some time to let the fresh air and sunlight come in.

Weekly Cleaning

Sunday is usually suitable for weekly cleaning — closets, doors, ceiling and walls can be cleaned; the utensils which are not used frequently should be washed weekly; the fridge or deep freezer should be defrosted and cleaned weekly to maintain its proper functioning.

Cleaning the Gas Stove

The stove should be wiped and cleaned daily with soap and warm water so that it is not stained, but it requires proper cleaning after a week or ten days to maintain its functioning. Method: (1) Boil water in a pan. (2) Turn off the main gas switch and disconnect it, if it is connected with a rubber pipe. (3) Take off the burners and stand; wipe the upper and lower parts of the stove; clean the burners with an old tooth brush to take out the sticky substance from its holes; wash with hot water and let them dry. (4) Wash the stand with luke-warm water and let it dry. (5) Clean the inner and outer sides of the stove with a wet cloth by using soap or vim, then wipe it with a dry cloth. (6) Put on the burners and stand and rub the stove with a soft cloth to let it shine. (7) Fix the pipe and turn on the gas switch. Note: if the stove is cleaned daily with vim and a wet cloth, it does not require such weekly cleaning, but it should be cleaned thoroughly for proper performance and maintenance.

Key Points

  • The health of the family depends upon the neat and clean utensils used for cooking and the cleanliness of the food.
  • It is necessary to keep the kitchen clean — the statement that it is not necessary is false.
  • The floor of the kitchen should be washed with hot water.
  • Daily cleaning of the stove is necessary — the statement that it is not necessary is false.
  • Turn off the main gas switch before cleaning the stove.
  • Good stove cleaning: gas supply disconnected before cleaning; proper time selected; knobs cleaned; greasy substance removed; precautionary measures taken; cleaning done in short time.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 — Budgeting (Living in the Family, Ch 4)

lessons.title: Budget: Definition, Principles and Types
lessons.notes_html:
Income and Expenditure

Money is required to meet the needs of life. Every family has to take care of the two aspects of its economic status, i.e. income and expenditure. Mostly the women are responsible for spending the money. A family cannot run well unless it keeps a balance between its income and expenditure, therefore budgeting is essential.

Definition of Budget

"Budget is a well thought out plan of income and expenditure." The main aim of the family budget is that the housewife plans her income and expenditure in such a way that the expenses do not exceed the income; in this way the important needs of the family such as health, education and economic status are taken care of, and maximum satisfaction is gained. A budget helps in avoiding unnecessary expenditures and in meeting emergency situations regarding money matters; above all, it reflects the management of the housewife.

Principles of Budgeting

(1) Important needs of life should be given first preference as compared to the less-important needs. (2) List down the total requirements of the family members. (3) An approximate estimate of the expenditure for total requirements should be made. (4) One should have a clear idea of the expected income for the period for which the budget is being planned. (5) There should be a balance between the income and expenditure. (6) The budget should be adjusted according to the requirements and alternatives suggested. (7) The budget should be flexible enough so that changes can be made easily as and when required. (8) The budget should be based on the basic principle: "cut your coat according to your cloth."

Types of Budget

A budget can be of two types: (1) Detailed budget — it includes all details of the account. (2) Outlined budget — it includes only important accounts; such budgets are mostly used in factories and other institutions. The household budget is a detailed budget; in this type of budget, detailed accounts of the expenditures are written daily, weekly or monthly.

Key Points

  • The economic status of a family has two aspects: income and expenditure.
  • To meet the needs of life money is required.
  • Important needs should be given first preference.
  • There should be a balance between the income and expenditure.
  • The budget should be based on the golden principle "cut your coat according to your cloth".

lessons.title: Making a Family Budget and Saving Money
lessons.notes_html:
Methods of Making a Family Budget

(1) Make a list of the total requirements of all the family members for a month; study the list and divide the requirements into three main categories: (a) most essential needs, (b) adjustable needs, (c) needs which can be postponed. (2) Be acquainted with the prices of all the items available in the market. (3) Compare the prices of different items in different markets. (4) Write down the daily expenditure in a register or a copy regularly, to have a clear idea about the unnecessary expenditure at the end of the month. (5) The budget should be flexible so that changes can be made. (6) Saving can be done by growing vegetables at home and raising poultry for eggs. (7) Saving can be done by carrying out the household work by all the family members. (8) Be acquainted with all sources of income. (9) Be acquainted with all the methods of saving.

Advantages of Budgeting

(1) Daily account keeping helps one to control the expenditures. (2) Knowledge of the prices of certain commodities helps in keeping a balance between income and expenditure. (3) No matter how less the income may be, expenditures can be controlled and some money can be saved for further needs. (4) The habit of over-spending on unnecessary items is controlled.

Saving

A certain amount of money which is saved after meeting all the needs of the family is called "saving". Unnecessary expenditure can be postponed from the actual budget in order to save some money for future needs, e.g. construction of the house, buying of a bicycle, scooter or car, or buying an essential item for the house; saving can also be done for the education of the children. Saving for the sake of saving is useless, because such saving is spent aimlessly without achieving any definite goal. Methods and principles of saving: (1) A definite amount for saving should be fixed and it should be saved. (2) Saving should be invested in profitable schemes, e.g. insurance, bonds, saving certificates, gold and land etc. (3) Family members can also help to increase the income by using their skills and abilities, e.g. stitching of clothes, driving a car personally, making decoration pieces, cooking and baking, growing vegetables and fruits at home, raising poultry and farming etc.

Key Points

  • Requirements are divided into three categories: most essential needs, adjustable needs, and needs which can be postponed.
  • Daily expenditure should be written in a register regularly.
  • Saving can be done by growing vegetables at home and raising poultry for eggs.
  • Saving should be invested in profitable schemes like insurance, bonds, saving certificates, gold and land.

lessons.title: Paper Flowers: Importance and Materials
lessons.notes_html:
Importance of Paper Flowers

Paper flowers play an important role to increase the beauty and decoration of a home. The technique of flower making is quite simple and easy. Such crafts increase our interest and likings. It increases our power of observation of the shapes and kinds of flowers and leaves found in nature; moreover, it increases our realization of the miracles and Greatness of God. Cloth, wool, foam, paper etc. are used for making flowers, and with practice one can make as many varieties of flowers as possible.

Material Required

(1) Crepe paper — available in rolls of different colours; lots of flowers can be made with one roll, and one roll of green crepe paper is sufficient for making enough leaves and branches. (2) Card-board — used for making the outline of the flowers according to the sizes required. (3) Wires — wires of different sizes and numbers are available in the market, mostly in rolls; the thickness of the wire depends upon the size and shape of the flower. (4) Glue — a special glue is used for joining different parts of a flower; it is available in bottles, and Peligum or UHU is also used, available in tubes. (5) Tape — tape is used for making stems; it is available in various colours, but for this purpose green tape is used. (6) Pair of scissors — a medium sized, pointed scissors is used for cutting the paper. (7) Wire snipper — used for cutting and turning the wires.

Key Points

  • Flower-making increases our interest; crepe paper is used for making paper flowers.
  • Crepe paper is available in different colours.
  • Green tape is used for making stems.
  • Wire snipper is used for cutting the wires.
  • Thin wire is used for making flowers (the book's true/false marks this true).

lessons.title: Making Sweet Peas and a Rose
lessons.notes_html:
Method — Sweet Peas

Material required: pink crepe paper, green crepe paper, wire, glue, pair of scissors, green tape, pencil, cardboard or thick paper. Method: (1) Trace the stencils on a cardboard as shown in the figures and cut. (2) One stem contains four flowers of sweet peas. (3) Two petals are required for one flower: fold the pink crepe paper eight times, place stencil A on it, trace and cut. (4) Turn its upper edges. (5) Fold the green crepe paper four times for making the sepals; place stencil B on it, trace and cut. (6) Lay two pieces together, fold in half; wrap wire around the base and tighten it by twisting the wire 2-3 times. (7) Curve the sepal outwards and glue in place. (8) Cut the tape from the centre lengthwise and wrap it. (9) Cut wires of 19 cms length; wind 3.5 cms over a pencil to make a vine. (10) Arrange the blooms around the wire by winding the tape or by pasting it with green crepe paper. Make more branches for a flower arrangement.

Method — Rose

Material required: red crepe paper, green crepe paper, wire, pencil, glue, green tape, cardboard or hard paper, pair of scissors. Method: (1) Make three stencils on a cardboard and cut. (2) Seven petals are used for making a rose: fold the red crepe paper seven times, place stencil A on it, trace and cut. (3) Place stencil B on the green crepe paper, trace and cut (for the sepal). (4) Four leaves are required for one stem, made by using a double layer of crepe paper: fold the green crepe paper eight times, place stencil C on it, trace and cut. (5) Crimp the petals. (6) Curl three petals. (7) Bend the wire; apply glue on it and wrap one petal on it. (8) Wrap the second and third petal in the same way. (9) Wrap all the petals. (10) Apply glue on the sepal and wrap. (11) Cut the green tape from the centre lengthwise and wrap it. (12) Cut the wire 8 cms long; wrap tape on it by leaving 3.5 cms wire. (13) Apply glue on the wire and attach two leaves together; attach all the leaves in this way. (14) Put three leaves together and join them by wrapping with the tape. (15) Join the leaves on the stem of the rose; curve the sepal outwards. One stem of one rose is complete; make other stems in the same way.

Key Points

  • Two petals are required for making one flower of sweet peas; one stem contains four flowers.
  • Seven petals are used for making a rose.
  • Cut a 1 cm wide strip of green crepe paper (for wrapping stems, as in the book's fill-in exercise).
  • Well-made paper flowers: made according to the instructions; petals of sweet peas neatly cut and fixed properly; flowers fixed properly on the stem; petals of rose neatly cut and fixed properly; rose fixed properly on the stem.
